title: 2001–2008: A Struggle
tagline: Dot-com bust · 9/11 and the War on Terror · Housing bubble · Global Financial Crisis

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: These were eight years that 'lived and died by real estate.' The fallout from the dot-com bust plus 9/11 made 2001 the first postwar recession to combine an external shock with an internal crisis. The Greenspan–Snow–Bernanke arc took rates from 6.5% all the way down to 1%, then back up to 5.25%. That single rate path shaped the entire life-cycle of the housing bubble.

Across the eight years the US endured two recessions (Mar–Nov 2001 and Dec 2007 – Jun 2009), two wars (Afghanistan in 2001, Iraq in 2003), two major corporate scandals (Enron in 2001, WorldCom in 2002), and a financial catastrophe (2008). The 'struggle' here looked manageable at the macro level, but the structural problems underneath kept piling up until they all detonated at once.

The era ended with Lehman's collapse, the AIG rescue, the $700 billion TARP, and zero interest rates. The 'New Economy' optimism of 1995–2000 was thoroughly broken by 2008, and 'the price of financialization' became the new consensus. These eight years were both the incubation and the explosion of the Global Financial Crisis — every institutional flaw (GLBA, the CFMA derivatives gap, rating-agency conflicts of interest, housing policy) came home to roost here.

items.strong: 2001–2003: Dot-com Bust, 9/11, and the War on Terror
items.body: The Nasdaq lost 78% over two and a half years from its March 2000 peak. The 2001 recession ran from March 1 to November 30 per NBER. After 9/11 the Fed cut aggressively (fed funds from 6.5% to 1.75% by December 2001, then to 1.0% by June 2003). Bush passed large tax cuts in 2001 and 2003 (EGTRRA and JGTRRA). Enron and WorldCom showed back-to-back accounting fraud, leading to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in July 2002. The Iraq War began in March 2003.

The Fed began 17 consecutive hikes in June 2004 (fed funds from 1.0% to 5.25%), but long-term rates barely budged — Greenspan called it the 'conundrum.' The housing bubble accelerated; subprime issuance went from $190 billion in 2003 to $600 billion in 2006. The Case-Shiller home-price index doubled between 2000 and 2006. Bernanke succeeded Greenspan in February 2006.

HSBC warned on subprime in February 2007 and New Century Financial filed for bankruptcy in April. In August BNP Paribas froze redemptions on three funds and the Fed injected $38 billion in emergency liquidity. The Fed began a cutting cycle in September 2007. JPMorgan acquired Bear Stearns in March 2008 with a $29 billion Fed backstop. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were placed into conservatorship in July 2008. Lehman filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 — a money market fund 'broke the buck' and AIG was bailed out by the Fed. The $700 billion TARP was signed in October 2008; zero rates and QE1 followed.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: Manufacturing Offshoring and Housing-Driven Growth
body: China's WTO accession reshaped global supply chains. After China joined in December 2001, US manufacturing employment fell from 17.3 million in 2000 to 13.7 million in 2008 — 3.6 million jobs lost in eight years. 'China Shock' research attributes roughly 40% of the decline in US manufacturing employment to this directly.

Financialization accelerated: finance and real estate value added went from 20% of GDP in 2000 to 21.5% in 2007. Financial-sector profits hit a historical peak of 35.6% of all corporate profits in 2003. 2003–2007 was the 'golden five years' for the financial industry, powered by the subprime securitization machine.

The household sector levered up: household debt as a share of disposable income rose from 95% in 2000 to 130% in 2007. The mortgage market grew from $5 trillion to $10 trillion. Subprime, Alt-A, and Jumbo (non-traditional) mortgages reached 40% of new originations in 2006.

Global imbalances: the US current-account deficit rose from $400 billion in 2001 to a peak of $800 billion in 2006 (6% of GDP). China's FX reserves grew from $200 billion in 2001 to $2 trillion in 2008. This 'global imbalance' was the macro backdrop to the 2008 crisis.

sections.heading: Key Failures of Financial Regulation
body: Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX), signed July 30, 2002, followed the Enron and WorldCom scandals. It strengthened corporate financial disclosure, made CEOs and CFOs personally accountable, and required internal-control audits — important corporate-governance reform, but it did not touch derivatives or the shadow banking system.

The SEC's 2003–2005 net-capital rule changes: in April 2004 the SEC let the five major investment banks (Goldman, Morgan Stanley, Merrill, Bear Stearns, Lehman) use internal models to calculate capital, taking leverage from about 15:1 to about 35:1 — a direct setup for the investment-bank failures of 2008.

Rating-agency conflicts of interest: Moody's, S&P, and Fitch handed out AAA ratings to enormous volumes of subprime MBS, with fees paid by issuers rather than investors. A large share of those AAA bonds were later downgraded to junk after the crisis.

The 'too big to fail' expectation crystallized: the Bear Stearns rescue in March 2008 and the Fannie/Freddie conservatorship on September 7 reinforced the market's belief that key financial institutions would always be backstopped — a political reason behind the authorities' choice to let Lehman fail.
